content:
We have mass spec: m/z 193.1103 (M+? likely molecular ion). Proton NMR shows signals: 1.20 (d, 3H) typical ethyl CH3; 2.85 (d, 2H) maybe CH2 next to carbonyl? 3.09 (qdd, 1H) maybe CH attached to CH3 and CH2? 3.81 (s, 3H) methoxy; aromatic 7.15 (ddd, 2H) and 7.92 (ddd, 2H) typical para-disubstituted benzene.

So likely a para-substituted aromatic with methoxy carbonyl (methyl ester) and an alkyl side chain maybe isobutyl? Let's deduce.

Molecular weight ~193.11. Let's compute formula possibilities. If we have aromatic ring C6H4 (para disubstituted). Add methoxy carbonyl: CO2Me = C2H3O2? Actually methyl ester of benzoic acid: CO2Me attached to ring: C7H6O2? Wait benzoic acid methyl ester (methyl benzoate) formula C8H8O2? Let's compute: C6H5-CO2Me = C8H8O2? Actually C6H5CO2CH3 = C8H8O2? Count: C6H5 + C(=O)OCH3 = C2H3O2 => total C8H8O2. Molar mass: C8=96, H8=8, O2=32 => 136. So not 193.

Add additional alkyl chain: maybe isopropyl? The NMR shows ethyl (CH3 d, CH2 d) and a CH (qdd). That suggests a CH attached to both CH3 and CH2? Could be CH attached to CH3 (doublet) and CH2 (doublet) and maybe coupling to something else. So maybe a sec-butyl group attached to aromatic? sec-butyl: CH(CH3)CH2CH3. But we see only one CH3 doublet (3H) at 1.20, a CH2 doublet at 2.85 (2H), and a CH quartet at 3.09 (1H). That matches CH attached to CH3 (doublet) and CH2 (quartet?) Actually CH (1H) coupling to CH3 (J~7) gives doublet, to CH2 (J~6.9) gives doublet of doublets? Observed qdd (quartet of doublet doublet). So sec-butyl attached to aromatic via CH (the chiral center). So aromatic attached to CH (bearing CH3 and CH2). The CH2 is adjacent to something else maybe carbonyl? But chemical shift 2.85 suggests benzylic CH2 attached to aromatic? Actually benzylic CH2 appears ~2.7-3.0. So maybe the side chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)-? But we have CH2 doublet (2H) at 2.85 coupling to CH (J 6.9). So CH2 is adjacent to CH. So chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)-? The CH attached to CH3 (doublet) and CH2 (doublet). So overall side chain is -CH(CH3)-CH2- attached to aromatic? But which carbon attaches to aromatic? Could be the CH2 attached to aromatic (benzylic) and then CH attached to CH3. That would give CH2 (2H) doublet coupling to CH (J~7). CH (1H) quartet (coupling to CH2 and CH3). CH3 doublet (3H) coupling to CH. That matches.

Thus structure: aromatic ring para-substituted with methoxy carbonyl (maybe methyl ester) and a side chain -CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., isopropylmethyl? Actually -CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's 2-carbon side chain with a methyl branch: -CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's 2 carbons plus a methyl branch = propyl group with branching at second carbon (i.e., 1-methylethyl? Wait -CH2-CH(CH3)- is ethyl attached to CH with methyl substituent, i.e., 1-methyl-ethyl? That's isobutyl? Isobutyl is -CH2-CH(CH3)2 (two methyls). Here only one methyl. So it's sec-butyl? sec-butyl is -CH(CH3)CH2CH3 attached via CH. Not match. Our pattern is aromatic-CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's 2 carbon chain with a methyl branch on the second carbon, but the chain ends at CH (attached to methyl). So overall side chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., 1-methyl-ethyl group). That's isopropyl? Actually isopropyl is -CH(CH3)2. Not same. So it's ethyl with a methyl substituent on the beta carbon: 1-methyl-ethyl (i.e., sec-propyl). That's "isopropyl"? Wait sec-propyl is CH(CH3)CH3? That's isopropyl. Hmm.

Let's think: aromatic-CH2-CH(CH3)-? The terminal carbon is CH attached to CH3 and maybe hydrogen only (no further substituents). So side chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)-H (i.e., 1-methyl-ethyl). That's "isopropyl" attached via CH2? Actually isopropyl is (CH3)2CH-. If attached via CH, you'd have (CH3)2CH- attached to aromatic. Not our case.

Our side chain: aromatic-CH2-CH(CH3)-H. That's "1-methyl-ethyl" group, also called "sec-propyl". So aromatic-CH2-CH(CH3)- (propyl attached via CH2). So overall substituent is -CH2-CH(CH3)- (C3H7). So formula for side chain: C3H7.

Now aromatic ring has two substituents: methoxy carbonyl (CO2Me) and this side chain. So total formula: aromatic C6H4 + CO2Me (C2H3O2) + side chain C3H7 = C11? Wait C6 +2+3 = C11. H: 4 +3+7 =14. O2. So C11H14O2. Molar mass: C11=132, H14=14, O2=32 => 178. Not 193.

But we also have maybe an extra carbonyl? The methoxy carbonyl could be part of an ester attached to aromatic via carbonyl (i.e., aromatic-COOCH3). That's methyl benzoate substituent, formula C8H8O2 as earlier. Add side chain C3H7 gives C11? Actually C8 + C3 = C11? Wait C8 + C3 = C11? No C8 + C3 = C11? That's wrong: 8+3=11, yes. H8+7=15, O2. So C11H15O2. Mass: 132+15+32=179. Still low.

Our mass is 193, 14 higher. Maybe there is an extra carbonyl (like acetyl) on side chain? But NMR shows only one carbonyl? IR not yet. Could be a methyl ester of a para-substituted phenylpropionic acid? Let's compute formula for para-methoxy carbonyl (CO2Me) plus propionic acid side chain? Actually side chain could be -CH2-CH2-COCH3? But NMR shows only one CH2 doublet, one CH quartet, one CH3 doublet. That suggests only three sets of aliphatic protons.

Maybe the side chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)-CO? But carbonyl would shift CH2 downfield maybe 2.3? Not 2.85. And would have extra carbonyl O.

Let's compute formula for C12H14O2? mass 194? C12=144, H14=14, O2=32 => 190. Not 193.

C12H16O2 = 192. C13H14O2 = 206. So 193 suggests maybe C12H13O2? mass 193? C12=144, H13=13, O2=32 => 189. Not.

Maybe there is a chlorine? But no halogen signals in NMR. Mass isotopic pattern shows M+1 194 (12.5%) typical for one chlorine? Chlorine gives ~33% M+2. Not.

So maybe formula C11H13O3? mass: C11=132, H13=13, O3=48 => 193. Yes C11H13O3 = 193. So maybe there are three oxygens: a methoxy carbonyl (CO2Me) plus an additional carbonyl (like acetyl) on side chain? That would be an aromatic ester with an acetyl group? But NMR shows only one methoxy singlet (3H) at 3.81, typical for OCH3. No other O-H. So maybe we have a phenyl acetate? Actually aromatic-COOCH3 (methyl ester) plus side chain with carbonyl? Could be phenylacetoacetate? Let's think.

C11H13O3 could be methyl 4-(1-methylpropyl)benzoate? That would be C12? Not.

Let's compute formula for methyl p-methylpropionate? Hmm.

Better approach: Use mass spec to get exact mass 193.1103. Let's calculate possible formula with C, H, O only. Use DBE formula: DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1. For C11H13O3: DBE = 11 - 13/2 +1 = 11 -6.5 +1 =5.5? Not integer, so not possible. Need integer DBE. So C11H14O3: DBE = 11 -7 +1 =5. So C11H14O3 mass: 132+14+48=194. Not 193.

C10H14O4: mass 120+14+64=198. No.

C9H10O5: 108+10+80=198.

C12H14O2: 144+14+32=190.

C12H16O2: 144+16+32=192.

C13H12O2: 156+12+32=200.

C13H14O2: 156+14+32=202.

So maybe formula includes nitrogen? C10H13NO2? mass: 120+13+14+32=179. Not.

C9H9ClO2? Cl 35.5 => mass 120+9+35.5+32=196.5.

Our exact mass 193.1103 suggests maybe C10H13NO3? mass: C10=120, H13=13, N=14, O3=48 => 195. Not.

Let's compute using typical isotopic pattern: M+1 194 intensity 12.5% suggests presence of one carbon (13C natural 1.1% per carbon). For 12 carbons, M+1 ~13% (12*1.1). So about 12 carbons. So formula likely C12H? O? Let's compute mass of C12H?O? to get 193.110. Subtract 12*12.000 =144. So remainder 49.110. O is 15.995 each. Suppose 2 O =31.99, remainder 17.12 => H count ~17.12 (since H 1.0079). So H ~17. So C12H17O2 mass: 144 + 17.134 +31.99 =193.124. Slight high. C12H16O2 = 144+16.128+31.99=192.118. So C12H16O2 is 192.118. Our mass 193.110 is between. Maybe C11H15O3: 132+15.119+47.985=195.104. Too high.

C13H13O2: 156+13.103+31.99=201.09.

Thus C12H16O2 seems plausible with M+1 13% (12 carbons). Our observed M+1 intensity 12.5% matches 12 carbons. So formula likely C12H16O2 (M 192.118). But observed M 193.110, off by 1.0. Could be M+H? Actually mass spec maybe shows [M+H]+? If using ESI positive mode, m/z could be (M+H)+. Then neutral mass = 192.110? Wait observed 193.110, subtract 1.007 = 192.103. That's close to C12H16O2 (192.118). Slight diff 0.015. Acceptable.

Thus neutral formula C12H16O2. DBE = C - H/2 +1 =12 -8 +1 =5. So 5 degrees unsaturation: aromatic ring (4) + carbonyl (1) =5. So structure: aromatic ring with one carbonyl (ester) and side chain with no additional unsaturation.

Thus we have para-disubstituted benzene with one substituent being methoxy carbonyl (ester) and other being -CH2-CH(CH3)- (propyl). That matches C12H16O2? Let's compute formula: aromatic C6H4, side chain C3H7, ester group CO2Me adds C2H3O2? Wait methyl ester attached via carbonyl to ring: -CO2CH3 adds C2H3O2 (C=O OCH3). So total C =6+3+2=11. H =4+7+3=14. O2. That's C11H14O2 = 178. Not match.

We need C12H16O2. So need one extra carbon and two extra hydrogens. Could be ethoxy carbonyl (COOCH2CH3) i.e., ethyl ester. That adds C3H5O2? Actually ethyl ester: -COOCH2CH3 adds C3H5O2? Let's count: carbonyl carbon (C), O, OCH2CH3 (C2H5). So total C3H5O2. So aromatic C6H4 + side chain C3H7 + ester C3H5 = C12H16O2. Yes! So it's ethyl ester of para-substituted benzoic acid with side chain.

Thus structure: para-ethyl benzoate? Wait ethyl benzoate has formula C9H10O2? Actually ethyl benzoate: C9H10O2? No, benzoic acid C7H6O2, plus ethyl adds C2H5 => C9H11O2? Let's compute: C6H5-CO2CH2CH3 = C9H10O2? Let's count: ring C6H5, carbonyl C1, O2, ethyl C2H5 => total C9? Actually C6+1+2=9, H5+5=10, O2. So C9H10O2, mass 150. Not.

Our compound has additional side chain C3H7 attached to ring, making C12H16O2. So it's ethyl 4-(propyl)benzoate? But side chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)-? That's isobutyl? Actually C3H7 attached directly to ring (alkyl). Could be n-propyl (CH2CH2CH3) gives C3H7. NMR pattern would be triplet, multiplet, etc not our pattern. Our pattern suggests CH2-CH(CH3)-H (sec-propyl). That's also C3H7. So para-sec-propyl ethyl benzoate.

SMILES: ethyl 4-(1-methylethyl)benzoate? Actually sec-propyl is CH(CH3)CH2- attached to ring via CH2? Wait sec-propyl attached via CH (the chiral carbon) to ring gives -CH(CH3)CH3 (isopropyl). Not our pattern. Our pattern is -CH2-CH(CH3)-H attached via CH2 to ring. That's "1-methyl-ethyl" group attached via CH2 (i.e., 1-methyl-ethyl substituent). That's "isobutyl"? Wait isobutyl is -CH2-CH(CH3)2 (two methyls). Not.

Our side chain is "sec-butyl"? sec-butyl attached via CH (the second carbon) to ring: -CH(CH3)CH2CH3. That would give CH (attached to ring) coupling to CH3 (doublet) and CH2 (quartet). CH2 would be further CH3 (triplet). But we only see one CH2 doublet, not triplet. So not sec-butyl.

Thus side chain is "propyl" attached via CH2: -CH2-CH(CH3)-H. That's "1-methyl-ethyl" (also called "isopropyl"? No). It's "propyl" with a methyl branch at the beta carbon, i.e., "2-methylpropyl"? Actually 2-methylpropyl is isobutyl (CH2-CH(CH3)2). Not.

Our side chain is "1-methyl-ethyl" which is same as "ethyl with methyl on beta carbon"? That's "propyl"? Wait propyl is CH2-CH2-CH3. If you put a methyl on the middle carbon, you get CH2-CH(CH3)-CH3 which is isobutyl? No that's 2-methylpropyl (isobutyl). So our side chain missing one CH3. So maybe the terminal carbon is a hydrogen (i.e., CH). So chain length 2 carbons plus a methyl branch: CH2-CH(CH3)-. That's "1-methylethyl"? Actually 1-methylethyl is isopropyl (CH(CH3)2). So not.

Thus maybe the side chain is -CH(CH3)2 attached via CH (i.e., isopropyl). That would give CH (1H) quartet? Actually CH attached to two equivalent CH3 groups gives septet (6 H coupling). Not observed.

Thus maybe the side chain is -CH2-CH2-CH3 (n-propyl) but NMR pattern could be misinterpreted: CH3 triplet (d?), CH2 quartet? But we have doublet for CH3, doublet for CH2, quartet for CH. So pattern matches -CH-CH2-CH3 where CH attached to CH3 (doublet) and CH2 (doublet) gives quartet? Actually CH coupling to both gives doublet of doublet, not quartet. But observed qdd suggests coupling to three equivalent protons (CH3) and two sets of 2H? Not.

Given limited time, propose SMILES: "CCOC(=O)c1ccc(cc1)CC(C)C"? That is ethyl 4-(sec-butyl)benzoate? Let's compute formula: ethyl (C2H5) + carbonyl C1O2 + ring C6H4 + sec-butyl C4H9 = total C13? C2+1+6+4=13, H5+4+4+9=22, O2. Too many.

Maybe simpler: "CCOC(=O)c1ccc(cc1)C(C)C"? That's ethyl 4-isopropyl benzoate? Isopropyl C3H7 attached via carbon (CH) to ring. Formula: C6H4 + C1O2 + C2H5 + C3H7 = C12H16O2 matches! Yes isopropyl attached via carbon (the central carbon) to ring: -C(CH3)2H. NMR for isopropyl: CH (septet) ~2.9, CH3 doublets ~1.2. But we have CH doublet? Actually isopropyl CH couples to 6 H (two methyls) gives septet (J~7). Not observed. But we have only one methyl doublet, suggests only one methyl.

Thus maybe the side chain is ethyl (CH2CH3) attached directly to ring: -CH2CH3. That would give CH3 triplet, CH2 quartet. Not match.

Given constraints, maybe the correct structure is ethyl 4-ethylbenzoate? That would be C11H14O2? Not.

Time low. Use search tool to find similar spectra? Could use search_by_smiles with candidate. Let's try search for "CCOC(=O)c1ccc(cc1)C(C)C".
